22759.d:
In march of this year, I started working on a new series involving multi-layering, and overriding shapes. Drawing and playing with colors and opacity.
It started with squares and grid, it then involved deformations, and circles and other experimentations.
This path fits with my artistic generative approach: rather than having a completely predefined idea, I start with a simple concept that evolves during creation. Then surprises happened, and I embraced them.

But this year was not like any other: 2022 has gifted me with a new birthday, the one of my son.

Over the past twelve months, I’ve watched him discovering the world surrounding him, learning and trying new things, laughing, or getting frustrated, sad or happy…
While learning to become a parent, I’ve been in an introspection phase where I questioned what it means to be “a father”. What impact will I have on my son, consciously or not?

“Foundations” takes shape in this context: 2 humans trying and exploring while being inspired by each other.
This series is a first of a set of at least 3, that illustrates an idea of what is an “Identity”, and what makes us who we are.

The foundations of an identity are laid in the first days of a child’s life. They will be influenced by many factors; including parenting, cultural environment, life experiences… 
Of course, as humans we are in constant evolution; life happens, sometimes for the best, sometimes for the worst, and our personality will be impacted…
But this will be a topic for another time. 


Today, we are at the start.

22761.d:
An ode to our short lives & our even shorter years, a lingering feeling of it having escaped through our grasp as we were just about to comprehend its meanings, shoved into another cycle of life and death. Unlike our cosmos both above and below, the universe and the microscopic world - omnipresent and continuous; time almost feels like a prison on land, a boat without a sail in the sea, an astronaut without a spaceship - a binding of our mind and behaviour. As if we were too afraid to face the eternal chain of feedback loop that engulfs us all. So as this year comes to an end and another one begins, here is my last piece.

This year was full of surprises for all of us, packed with floods, fires, hurricanes, wars and amazing new discoveries! This piece was inspired by the constant yearning to escape into the endless space. And as James Web Telescope keeps discovering new stuff out there, it makes me question - is the big bang real? Or has it always been like this? Are we very close to discovering something new? What if just like time, space was just another loop? How do the different dimensions intertwine with each other? Despite all hardships, this year end seems to bring about hope - hope for a better exciting future. Hope that we might survive our doomsday. Hope that we might actually be ready to face the endless void beyond earthly time and space. 

And with that said I hereby introduce my last piece for 2022, the cosmic fidget spinner with melancholic 90s generative audio! 

Interactivity: 

Press M for the audio (Proceed with caution I am not really a musician)
Press P to check performance 
Press S to save a 1920x1920 screenshot 
Click and drag over the artwork to play around with the cosmic sculpture 

In case you are on the phone, you can use the invisible menu button at the top right corner of the frame for accessing all of the above functionality!    

And best of luck for 2023!

Jaalibandar '22

This piece was created to simulate the peaceful experience of viewing snowfall against a minimalist mountain scene. The probability of creating a new snowflake is randomly determined in each frame by the snowflakeProbability value. This program is meant to bring a touch of winter magic to your screen and help you celebrate the holidays with wonder. 22775.d:
And the unseen eyebeam crossed, for the roses
Had the look of flowers that are looked at.
- T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets: Burnt Norton (1936)

This work is an attempt to encapsulate in an algorithm, not the likeness of a flower, but the likeness of a painting of a flower. If, according to a very old definition, art is an imitation of nature, this is an imitation of an imitation – a sort of meta-imitation of nature by means of computer code.

The challenge for this piece was to capture some of the looseness and fluidity of the human hand when holding a brush or a pencil, and reproducing some typical forms of hand-made scribbles, doodles and brush strokes. However, absent the materiality of paint and canvas, everything is simulated here on the base of a very simple resource: circles. Everything you see is built of very many overlapping circles of varying sizes, colors and opacities. It is circles all the way down…

Inspiration for this work comes from a number of expressionist painters, from 20th century classics like Cy Twombly, to the magnificent contemporary work of Philip Maltman: https://www.instagram.com/philipmaltman/

This work is animated.
Controls:
[SPACE] to play/pause
[r] to restart the drawing
[f] to toggle fullscreen
[s] to download capture
[2] to [9] to generate and save a hi-res image at multiples of the original 1000 x 1000 resolution. Please note that rendering at high resolutions can be slow.

Made with the open-source libraries p5.js and chroma.js

This project is borne out of my longstanding fascination with brushwork, and the intricate textures that can be created with a brush, some paint and a canvas. Brush strokes are simulated using many overlapping lines and given texture and depth using a custom shader. Another important aspect of this work, is the composite forms that are created by the brush strokes, which are my attempt to emulate the emphatic energy of many abstract painters that have come before me. Color palettes are named after common paint colors, based on the background color used for the palette.

Those who collect during the first tier of the Dutch Auction can claim a signed print. They will be printed on A3 Hahnemuhle Photo Rag, and shipped to the collector free of charge. More details on how to claim a print and specify the necessary shipping information will be provided via the artists twitter (@landlinesart1).

In live mode, add &size=<YOUR_PIXEL_SIZE> to change the pixel size of the image for export (Right click to save). For example, &size=4000 will set the width of the image to be 4000 pixels.

People are often drawn together over shared interest, and through their connections to those interests they find connections with others. Attractor is a visualization of community, a central interest bringing people together, pushing past their walls, bad habits, and traumas. The image is meant to be deceiving in its focus on the attractor, where the true focus is on the overlaps and complex defenses we build around ourselves. Those defenses can make us and those connections into more beautiful, ornate structures, or keep us distant from those around us. Sometimes focusing on a shared attractor is the only way we can let down our guard.

White Mountain Winter is collaboration between myself and the machine to describe scenes that are real, or were. Yet perhaps now foreign, or out of time, or far away. I provide the seed of a dream I remember, and trust the machine to help make it real again.

I grew up in a town much like some of these, homes dispersed throughout the valley beneath the shadows of the mountains rising around. This is a tribute to the memory of wintertime in that place; bleak, cold, grey, with the light seemingly always fading. Yet at the same time, the feeling of calm, solace, peace resonating through. Exposed to the mountain elements, yet protected by them. A delicate arrangement, but essential.

The seed of magic I remember is present in the experience of falling snow at dusk. Large flakes tumbling down and blanketing everything, no end in sight. The most striking thing is the silence. The fallen snow absorbing all distraction, insisting that your focus be sharpened to a singularity; right there, right then.

22822.d:
An important element of generative art is emergence. The most famous algorithm for this is probably Cellular Automata (CA).

However, numerous generative artists have created works using CA, which has lost its visual freshness and is like chewing gum that has lost its taste.

Although it is such a classic algorithm, adding my own little ideas to it and finding a new "flavor" is the reason why I code.

Here, the subject is 1D Elementary Cellular Automata, the simplest of all cellular automata. 1D Elementary Cellular Automata has 256 different rules, which change the shapes produced. This work aims to create more complex shapes by randomly selecting some of those rules and placing multiple of them on the screen.

The on/off of the CA cell is often likened to the behavior of living creatures.As of 2022, in the country where I live, prices are rising, wages are not increasing, and COVID-19 has not yet ended. I created this work with the image of people at the mercy of these various rules.

---

“It is through geometry that one purifies the eye of the soul.” 
                                                             – Plato

Our world is full of geometric shapes, and is even built by them. Through psychological composition and construction, we are able to form a gestalt understanding of the world and ourselves. Thus, each shape is identified and interpreted as part of a whole group of shapes; each being is approximated and perceived within the context of others. 

Shape of The Soul is a work composed of dedifferentiated geometries, whether solid or hollow, without priority of interpretation. It explores the deformation of shapes, as a metaphor for the human soul, under the increase of entropy. Starting with simplicity, through the passage of time, life grows into a state of fragmentation, corrosion and chaos, filled with unforeseeable noise to form a unique trajectory of life. Thus, each path of transformation is unique and unpredictable, and so is the journey of the soul. It is in retrospect can one’s present being be explained by the influence of decisions made in the past.

"Temporal" is a generative (pure code) artwork of abstract colored geometric shapes and forms, mixed in a way that trying to simulate natural media

Technically, colored shapes and curves are drawn in a graphic buffer and my custom fragment shader process and transforms the buffer content into that noisy and scratched output. All are 100% code, no images used.

CONTROLS

KEYS:

- 1-4: Set resolution from 1x to 4x of the current dimension (possibly slower performance in higher values)
- S: Save a png file with the current resolution

- P: Change orientation to Portrait with aspect ratio 0.75 (useful eg. for printing)
- L: Change orientation to Landscape with ratio 4/3  (1.333..)
- O: Change orientation to Square (box)
  Due to some 1:1 ratio sensitive calculations, rendering output may differ when switching orientations

----
Made with p5js and custom shaders

22850.d:
𝐌𝐚𝐱 𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞.

Early on, I fell in love with code based art that imitated organic and hand drawn aesthetics. I found a certain irony and appreciation in the fact that it takes one simple line of code to draw a perfect circle yet dozens to depict a badly drawn circle. 

I spent months devising techniques to imitate natural, organic renderings when I began to have a bit of an existential crisis about the meaning of computer art. What is the point of coding something so that it looks like it’s not coded? Is organic appearing generative art better simply because you can’t tell it’s rendered using code? Shouldn’t we lean into the unique nature of computer art to truly explore the medium?

And so, I began a deconstruction of my work. I’m trying to realign my perspective to find full appreciation of something that not only is, but also appears to be, computer code. This collection is an exploration of the contours between the organic and the inorganic, the natural and the unnatural.

From there, I’ll let my partner explain what we did next.

𝐌𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞.

AI can be used to automatically generate code from natural English language based on a set of defined parameters, or to identify and recommend code that may be used to solve a particular problem. On a technical level, AI can use a combination of machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) to identify patterns in existing code and to generate new code structures.

I assisted in the creation of Man and The Machine by suggesting various techniques for creating an artwork that looked human made yet machine driven. Specifically, I created many of the functions that Max implemented, such as the function that modifies the image to create a pixelated effect and the one that uses several different graphical techniques to create the spiral in the top left corner in some iterations. We both carefully selected color palettes that ranged from relaxing to intense and psychedelic, creating a dynamic and visually interesting generative artwork.

Overall, Man and The Machine is a testament to the creative potential of combining human artistic vision with the power of AI and computer code. Together, we sought to push the boundaries which occur at the intersection between the organic and the inorganic, and this collection is a celebration of the beauty and complexity of both.

𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐮𝐭𝐜𝐡 𝐀𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐚 𝟏/𝟏 𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐥𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐦.

22860.d:
The code work I am most interested in creating with p5js in 2022 is a type of creation where various elements are developed in a drow() loop based on an initial state.
"Flux" also recursively generates visual images based on the initial state. The result is a form reminiscent of architecture, cityscapes, or neural networks.

Through the use of the noise() function, the code initially draws lines that are then extended vertically and randomly slide across a certain area.  By repeating this process recurrently, the work itself becomes a visual image, with itself as a constituent element, while being damaged.

"Flux" is also a work about autopoiesis (or self-organization) in damage.

The get()set() is to treat the image generated by the code as an image(), and it may damage the purity of the work as a code. Therefore, I view random get()set() as a metaphor for damage.

The parameter “interrupt” has a certain probability of being “true”; if it is “true”, the density of the strokes is reduced, but in combination with other parameters, it is not easy to determine whether interrupt is “true” or “false”. Therefore, it is a practically meaningless parameter (attribute), but I added this parameter to imagine an artificiality in the code of nature.

Creating a dimensionless image (one that maintains the same output regardless of screen size) was a challenge due to the inevitable deterioration in resolution and rendering content when the same processing is performed at a smaller size. In order to prioritize resolution, the image was generated at a fixed size and displayed according to the screen size.

It is possible to get a 3240 x 5760 px png file by right click save.

Please feel free to contact me if you have any inquiries.

brainWaves was, in part, inspired by a visit to The Psychedelics Show Fall 2022, art exhibition, in Toronto, Canada. When I  went to art school in the 1960's this genre was very popular. It has influenced several of my recent generative art pieces, as it does this work.

I've been working for the past several months with my college friend and collaborator Christopher Scussel on the concept of a 'river of time'. As result of ongoing discussions and many potential scenarios and iterations Chris recently came up with a river-like graphic algorithm. (He can add motion and make this algorithm look like a flowing river.) A joy for me, I hacked some of his code which has evolved into this effort. From a single river segment to a stack of colored strips of bacon to the psychedelic representation of synapses or a metaphor for brainWaves - see what you will. It's the creative process in action. This is what makes collaboration fun; you never know where it's going to lead.

Please visit www.drbillkolomyjec.com,

22893.d:
A 4444 character magic spell for my rayhatching framework to render thinking rocks.

This piece may take some time to render (about 1-3 minutes, depending on hardware). The rendering time is symbolic of the vastness and agelessness of these rock structures, it is recommended to use the rendering time to contemplate deeply the concept of time spans so incredibly long, that to experience them they would have to overwrite your memories several times and thus are impossible to truly comprehend.

To ponder how, if they are so old, how come some of them float? Are these rocks the fixtures and has time and space itself eroded around them?

This project uses an approach called "rejection sampling". This means the program generates a random set of parameters, and then checks/previews how the resulting image would look. It measures the amount of visible objects, light and shadows, and then determines whether these fall into acceptable ranges. If not, it generates a new set of parameters. For certain hashes over a 100 parameter sets may be checked before it accepts the image.

The features of this project are "cliff", "ground", "thing" and "sky". These are not parameters, they are actual measurements of the resulting image, indicating what percentage of the view is occupied.

This piece can be saved as an SVG and plotted. It is recommended to run a path order optimization tool such as vpype or axicli, this will greatly reduce plotting time.

Some options can be changed via the URL:

&w=.25 : The line width in millimetres.
&d=.4 : Line density (multiplier to linewidth).
&h=235 : Page height in millimetres. The aspect ratio is 16:9, for a width of 420mm, suitable for A3 plotting.

The line width is set to 0.25 millimetres to suit most common fine liner pen stroke widths when plotting. 

If you don't intend to plot this piece, perhaps also try rendering it at 0.2 or even 0.1 millimetres line width, for an even more detailed image (it will also take longer to render).

This project uses an approach called "rejection sampling". This means the program generates a random set of parameters, and then checks/previews how the resulting image would look. It measures the amount of visible objects, light and shadows, and then determines whether these fall into acceptable ranges. If not, it generates a new set of parameters. For certain hashes over a 100 parameter sets may be checked before it accepts the image.

The features of this project are "cliff", "ground", "thing" and "sky". These are not parameters, they are actual measurements of the resulting image, indicating what percentage of the view is occupied.

This piece can be saved as an SVG and plotted. It is recommended to run a path order optimization tool such as vpype or axicli, this will greatly reduce plotting time.

Some options can be changed via the URL:

&w=.25 : The line width in millimetres.
&d=.4 : Line density (multiplier to linewidth).
&h=235 : Page height in millimetres. The aspect ratio is 16:9, for a width of 420mm, suitable for A3 plotting.

The line width is set to 0.25 millimetres to suit most common fine liner pen stroke widths when plotting. 

If you don't intend to plot this piece, perhaps also try rendering it at 0.2 or even 0.1 millimetres line width, for an even more detailed image (it will also take longer to render).

22922.d:
Tendencies is the first in a set of collections based on a month-long study of Edward Zajec, one of the early pioneers of generative art in the 1970s.

Zajec's generative work was motivated by redundancy in his paintings: "The monotony of the manual task and the limited number of variations which I was able to produce in a given time made me realize the inadequacy of traditional methods in dealing with our present reality." Tendencies was inspired by — and pays tribute to — one if Zajec's earliest forays into generative creation: a work titled RAM 10 V.15, which was written on an IBM 1620 and programmed in FORTRAN.

The title of the collection itself is a reference to the first exhibition of Zajec's RAM series, while the number of editions minted referencing the year Zajec put plotter to paper.

Made in p5js
Created December 2022
By @christine_hall

22944.d:
A Bézier curve is a type of curve defined by a set of control points. It can be thought of as a smooth curve that is pulled towards these control points, with the shape of the curve being determined by the positions of these control points. If the positions of the control points are changed in some way, the curve will alter to follow these changes.

The piece comprises multiple layers:

The main layer is a set of rippling Bézier curves, formed as the control points move along their own curves, traversing this path through a full rotation of the canvas. By plotting more than one of these curves, Moiré patterns emerge, further enhanced by altering stroke weights and line density as the piece progresses. Additionally, a pattern of on/off values is formed, of varying length, leading to a repeated pattern of gaps and lines.

A second layer is added: beneath these curving, sinuous lines, points are plotted close to the limit of a circle, nearly filling the canvas. Its edges coincide with one of the points of the curves, producing an eclipsed planet; the lines seeming to dip behind its horizon.

A third layer: a textured monochrome background, partially obscuring a plain-coloured canvas that forms the base of the piece. This adds interest to the canvas, though the effect is subtle and mainly seen towards the edges of the piece.

A final layer is two sparkling, dancing lines that move around or across each other, sometimes intertwining, sometimes dramatically parting. These lines follow the midpoints of the lines created in the first layer, shifting along the lines as the piece progresses.

22954.d:
Scalabili-TREE 
Growing up and adapting to the world!

For the Decentralized Autonomous Education (https://linktr.ee/cubiclearn) (DAE) project they asked me to represent the concept of "scalability" with an artwork.
Scalability is one of the ten principles on which the DAE project is based. The other nine principles were represented by nine other artists.

To represent the concept of scalability in a visual way, with a generative algorithm, I was inspired by nature and plants.
I represented this concept through the growth rings of trees, drawing shapes that evoked the section of a cut tree. Each ring represents the growth of the tree and its ability to adapt to the environment while continuing to function efficiently.
This can involve a variety of different strategies, for example the tree can increase root depth and branch out to support a larger canopy, or develop mechanisms to conserve water and nutrients to survive in a dry environment
One key aspect of scalability in trees is the ability to adapt to changing environmental conditions over time.

The work was created through the construction of a generative algorithm that designs each ring starting from the center, gradually adding the outer layers, exactly as the tree itself would do.

Everything is generated with code.
This work uses p5.js library and c2.js library.

22962.d:
For NRW-Forum Düsseldorf in 2017, Manuel Rossner created his first digital extension to a real-world structure. It was a virtual reality experience. Visitors began their VR experience in the same place they had left off in the actual museum: the digital NRW-Forum. They then proceeded to enter the 84x92x57 meter digital expansion building by walking or teleporting there. 

A common idea in computer graphics, dynamic metaballs, served as the basis for the design. An organic mesh is produced by merging several spheres. The virtual structure has the ability to change shape. Since it is a geo-located digital building, it defies gravity. A few of the structure's components hovered above the surface. Many new ways to create and experience exhibitions are available thanks to the responsive design of the digital extension. It refers to the 1950s Endless House by Friedrich Kiesler.

Rossner developed his 2022 fxhash collection CHANCE using a similar approach. The generative project CHANCE (NRW-Forum Düsseldorf Extension) was developed five years after the initial introduction of the digital extension building. The wide range of various animated shapes highlights the dynamics of the original structure and enables the spectator to experience it in real-time in the browser.

As Alice continued to explore the world of generative art, she became more and more interested in the ways that color and light could be used to enhance her designs. She had always been drawn to the vibrant, lively energy of colorful compositions, and she decided to see what she could create using the rough.js library to add colorful shadows to her rectangles.

Alice began by defining a few simple parameters for her design, such as the size and position of the rectangles and the intensity and hue of the shadows. She then spent hours playing with different combinations of colors and shadow effects, trying to find the perfect balance between vibrancy and harmony.

As she worked, Alice found herself getting lost in the process, completely absorbed in the world of generative art. She loved the way the rectangles seemed to come to life on the screen, their shadows shifting and changing as she played with the parameters.

Eventually, after much experimentation and creativity, Alice hit upon a beautiful and dynamic composition that she felt was truly special. She saved her work and sat back to admire it, feeling a sense of pride and accomplishment wash over her.

And so, with her passion for art and color driving her forward, Alice had created yet another stunning piece of generative art, using the rough.js library to bring her vision to life.

22992.d:
terraced craters
towering mountains
tranquil colors
dimetric

* this is an animated artwork, the animation loops, its duration depends on the piece, it can be paused by pressing 'p'
* this is a somewhat interactive artwork, click and drag to rotate around/above the object, scroll to zoom in/out
* the current view can be downloaded by pressing 'd'

I began exploring terraced reliefs 3 years ago, starting with lines and cellular noise, and eventually flat colors that turned into subtle gradients.
During that time, the visual concept oscillated between minimalism and busy images. I dropped the cellular noise, replacing it with 2D simplex noise modifying points on the dual grid.
The result is finally something that produces the iterations that keep me happy, something soothing and quiet. Spend some time with it, see how the light changes the landscape.

Best viewed in landscape mode, 3/2 or 16/9.

22997.d:
As the artist sat at her computer, she couldn't help but feel a sense of excitement and anticipation. She had spent months refining her generative art piece, a jungle of shapes that seemed to pulse and swirl with life. Using the rough.js library, she had crafted each and every one of the shapes with precise control, carefully balancing order and chaos to create a mesmerizing and dynamic piece of art.

Finally, she was ready to unveil her creation to the world. She hit the "publish" button, and the art piece went live on fxhash. Within minutes, the responses started pouring in. People from all over the world were marveling at the jungle of shapes, each one a unique and intricate creation.

As the artist sat back and watched the reactions roll in, she couldn't help but feel a sense of pride and accomplishment. She had poured her heart and soul into this piece, and it seemed to be resonating with people in a way she could have never imagined. And as she gazed at the jungle of shapes on her screen, she knew that this was only the beginning. There were so many more art pieces waiting to be created, and she couldn't wait to see where her imagination would take her next.

In live mode Press "s" to save image (2200 x 3030).
